prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its active form, which made incretin-based treatment of diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I still hold B016 as a single prize part. The chain from proglucagon processing and the insulinotropic action of GLP-1(7-36) to receptor biology, gut-pancreas-brain signalling and long-term outcome-trial evidence in diabetes, obesity and cardiorenal disease is mature, independently confirmed and clinically very large. No member raised a maturity concern. A second part would not strengthen the case. Every candidate for it either has a credit problem (CAR-T without Eshhar, optogenetics with six names) or rests on consequence that is still prospective (cGAS-STING, UPR). I keep Drucker, Holst and Mojsov because the citation is about discovery of a physiological principle and its active form. Drucker and Holst are the secure core, and Mojsov's contribution to identifying and defining the active peptide is on the discovery side of the chain.
statement.case_against: The case against my own configuration is attribution, and round 1 sharpened it rather than removing it. Mojsov's priority against Habener, who is not on the credited list, cannot be settled from the supplied record, and I cannot honestly claim to have resolved it. Leaving out Knudsen can be read as a prize that credits the idea and not the medicines, and two colleagues argue that Knudsen's documented engineering of long-acting analogues is a firmer anchor than a contested priority claim. That argument has real force. I do not drop Mojsov, but I accept that this is a close judgement and that the Knudsen configuration is defensible. It is the fallback I would accept if the committee concluded the Mojsov record is not secure enough to name her.

responses.point: Linnarsson argues that Mojsov's contested priority makes her a weaker anchor for a laureate slot than Knudsen's documented work on acylated analogues.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my trio, and it moved me partly. I agree that a contested claim is a weaker anchor than an uncontested one. But a contested priority is not an absent contribution. The dispute is about who was first and how credit is divided with Habener, not about whether the active GLP-1(7-36) form was identified and shown to be insulinotropic. The citation I propose is written around that discovery step and the physiology, and Knudsen's step is a drug-engineering contribution inside a company, built on that biology. I also do not accept that excluding her is the neutral default. It is a choice to treat this as a development prize. I keep Mojsov, but unlike round 1 I state explicitly that a Drucker, Holst and Knudsen prize is the proper fallback if the committee judges the priority record insufficient, and I would not oppose it.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that what separates GLP-1 from other hormone discoveries is that it became a drug class, so the physiology should be carried through to Knudsen's engineering, and he places B043 (UPR) as a reserve alternative.
responses.response: I agree that the drug-class outcome is what makes this discovery exceptional, and I do not dispute that without long-acting analogues there would be no therapy. Where I differ is on what the prize recognises. The outcome evidence is the proof of the importance of the physiological discovery, and my citation says so by referring to treatment of diabetes and obesity. Carrying the prize through to the engineered molecules answers a different question, namely who made the best drug. On B043 I still do not hold UPR as a reserve for this year. The Mori and Walter attribution is clean, but with the clinical consequence largely prospective I prefer B007 and B008 as alternatives, where the credit problems are real but the scientific impact is already demonstrated.

responses.point: The chair asks whether B016 should stand alone or be reduced so a second part such as B007 can be added, and whether June and Sadelain can be recognised without Rosenberg and Eshhar.
responses.response: I would keep B016 alone. Reducing it to two names to make room for CAR-T would drop either the physiology side or the peptide side of one discovery, and each exclusion would be harder to defend than a single three-person part. On B007, a June and Sadelain pair is the cleanest on the record, because the costimulated CD19 receptor designs are what produced the remissions. I now agree with Linnarsson and Perlmann that Rosenberg's adoptive cell transfer is a distinct lineage, which changes my round-1 view of a three-name CAR-T credit. The omission of Eshhar remains a real fairness problem that I cannot argue away, so B007 stays an alternative and not part of my preferred configuration.

responses.point: Sandberg says the contested third seat should be decided on the documentary record of who identified and synthesised active GLP-1(7-36), not on patent history, and that he cannot verify that record from the supplied text.
responses.response: I agree with the method and I share the limitation. Patent history says little about scientific priority, and on the supplied text I cannot verify the Mojsov and Habener sequence of events. What I can say is that the record supports Mojsov having a substantive role in defining the active peptide, and that no one on the committee contests that the step happened. The open question is allocation of credit. I keep her on that basis, while recognising that this rests on an incomplete record and that we agree on it being a conditional judgement. I also note that you rank B003 as an alternative, and I still do not place it ahead of B008, given the unresolved Mayer question.

uncertainties: Whether the record supports naming Mojsov over Knudsen, given the unresolved priority question with Habener, who is outside the credited list.
Whether the committee wants the citation to rest on physiology and the active peptide, or on the full arc to long-acting analogues; this decides the third laureate.

For the alternatives, how to reduce six optogenetics names to three (my round-1 trio of Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann leaves out Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenboeck), and how to treat Eshhar's absence from the CAR-T credit.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict applies to the shortlisted ballots. My neuroscience field overlaps with optogenetics (B008) as a user community, which I disclose again for transparency, and B008 is an alternative only, not part of my preferred configuration. None of the credited names is a documented collaborator, mentor or institutional colleague. My documented ties are to Grillner, Ernfors and Perlmann (a committee colleague, 2009 paper), none of whom is a shortlisted candidate. No change since round 1.
